EXTRA CLASS · KIDS GAMES

Every game, with its rules on the card.

The afternoon-saver class: twenty-six classic games walk the whole day in tour order — throwing and aiming, running and freezing, table games and turns, quiet find-and-solve games, acting and guessing, and the sidewalk classics — and every guide below is a kid-followable how-to-play, right on this page.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Every game a childhood needs — with the rules on the card.

The Kids Games class is a bonus class, kept beside the main learning path like the Kitchen Helper and the Doctor Visit: the regular classes stay the core sequence, and this one is for the afternoons when somebody says I don’t know what to play. Twenty-six classic games — balloon keep-up, hide and seek, tic-tac-toe, treasure hunt — each one on its own card, and each card opens a simple guide a kid can follow: what you need, how to play, step by step, and one way to make it fresh tomorrow.

The games run in tour order on purpose. The throwing and rolling games come first, because aiming is where little arms start; then the running-and-freezing games that empty a room of wiggles; then the table games that teach waiting a turn; the quiet find-and-solve games for the rainy shelf; the acting games for loud imaginations; and the last group belongs outside — chalk, pavement and a rope on a swing.

THE GAMES, SIX WAYS TO PLAY

Twenty-six cards, six kinds of play.

Twenty-six games in six groups, in the order a real game afternoon unfolds. Every how-to-play guide is right here on this page — the original card beside the simple kid-followable steps, game after game.

Throw, roll & aim

Games where something flies: the balloon that must stay up, the beanbag, the ball, the rings and the paper plane — and the target waiting for every throw.

Balloon Keep-UpBeanbag TossBowlingHoop TossPaper Plane Target
Run, chase & freeze

The big-movement classics: hiding and seeking, freezing mid-dance, passing fast, walking the chairs and stopping on a word.

Duck, Duck, GooseFollow the LeaderFreeze DanceHide and SeekHot PotatoMusical ChairsRed Light, Green Light
Table & take turns

Sit-down games that teach waiting your turn: grids and discs, cards and pairs, a magnetic pond and one very decisive hand game.

BingoFishingFour in a RowMemory MatchRock, Paper, ScissorsTic-Tac-Toe
Look, find & solve

The quiet-power games: tracing mazes, joining pieces, catching the sneaky changes and following the clues to the treasure.

MazePuzzleSpot the DifferenceTreasure Hunt
Act, guess & listen

Games your imagination runs: acting without a single word and obeying only the commands that carry the magic words.

CharadesSimon Says
Playground & outdoors

The sidewalk classics: chalk numbers under hopping feet and a rope that keeps swinging to its own chant.

HopscotchJump Rope
THE CLASS GAME

Game Day: let the stack decide.

Stack the cards face down. Draw the top one, read its guide together, play the game — and the winner of each game draws the next card. That is Game Day, and it runs itself: the stack decides everything, the winning gets a crown (and the drawing job), and the afternoon ends only when the stack ends. Losing practice is built right in: short rounds, loud good-games, immediate rematches.

SAME GAME, TWO NAMES

Tic-tac-toe and noughts and crosses. Both are right.

Games travel lighter than words do — the same game grows a new name on every shore, and this class says so out loud. Tic-tac-toe is noughts and crosses in the UK; the jump rope is a skipping rope; the paper plane flies as a paper aeroplane; freeze dance is musical statues across the ocean; the balloon game rides the UK playground word keepy-uppy; and the disc-dropping grid most homes call Connect Four is simply four in a row here — the generic name, playable with buttons on a drawn grid. Whichever your family says, your child hears both — and learns early that games, like words, come in kinds.

Every guide has a matching flashcard in the library: the original artwork as a printable card with a download button and short notes for grown-ups. Keep the five sit-down cards in a basket near the couch — on a gray afternoon, the basket is the plan.

Age ranges are a guide, not a test. Start with the game your child loves best, follow the giggle, follow the child — and say the rule out loud before every game: a child who can say the rule can run the game with friends.

TEACHER’S LESSON

How this class is taught.

By the end of this class: your child has met all 26 cards in Kids Games, said each word with you and tried one small activity from the lesson.

  1. 01
    Welcome

    “Hello! Today we are learning about Kids Games. We have 26 cards, and we will look at them one at a time.”

    How: Sit side by side with the cards in front of you. Keep your voice warm and unhurried, and let your child touch the cards.

  2. Cards 1–10
  3. 02
    Card 1 · Balloon Keep-Up

    “Balloon keep-up! The balloon is sleepy and wants to fall — tap it gently to wake it up. One tap, two taps — do not let it touch the floor!”

    How: Count the taps out loud: how many saves before it lands? Tomorrow, try the harder way — one hand only, or everyone sits on the floor and the balloon may never go higher than your head.

  4. 03
    Card 2 · Beanbag Toss

    “Beanbag toss! Hold it flat in your hand, look at the hole, step forward and — throw! Did it land in? A beanbag on the floor still counts as a practice throw.”

    How: Start close and step back one heel-toe step after every success. Three in the middle hole earns a cheer; three misses in a row means you move closer instead — the game bends to the thrower.

  5. 04
    Card 3 · Bowling

    “Bowling! The pins are standing in a triangle. Roll the ball low and slow — rrroll — and down they go! Count how many fell, then stand them up again.”

    How: Set the pins up together — that is half the game. Take turns: one roll each, count the fallen pins out loud, and the fell-then-standing rhythm keeps everyone busy even while waiting.

  6. 05
    Card 4 · Hoop Toss

    “Hoop toss! Hold the ring flat like a frisbee, look at the peg, and let it fly. Ten points if it lands near, fifty if you ring the far one!”

    How: Keep score with a tally on paper — a mark for every ten. Five rounds each, then add the tallies together and crown the ring champion (and offer a rematch immediately, as tradition demands).

  7. 06
    Card 5 · Paper Plane Target

    “Paper plane target! Fold the plane, stand behind the line, and let it fly at the bullseye. Did it land close? One point. Did it land in the circle? Three points!”

    How: Fold two planes and race them — the winner is whichever lands nearest the target. Try throwing soft, then hard, and discover which way flies straighter. Every flight teaches the next fold.

  8. 07
    Card 6 · Duck, Duck, Goose

    “Duck, duck, duck... GOOSE! Run around the ring and back to the empty spot before the goose catches you! Sit down fast — the goose is quick today.”

    How: Play with the gentle rule that the tapper walks and the goose runs. After a few rounds, let your child be the tapper — choosing who to pick is the secret, delicious power of this game.

  9. 08
    Card 7 · Follow the Leader

    “Follow the leader! March, march — now hop! Now tiptoe like a mouse — shh! Everybody copies the leader, and when I say ‘new leader‘, it is someone else’s turn to decide the moves.”

    How: Take the leader job yourself first and make the moves easy to copy: touch your nose, spin once, walk backward. Then hand the crown over. A quiet child often leads loudest on round two.

  10. 09
    Card 8 · Freeze Dance

    “Freeze dance! When the music plays — dance, dance, dance! When it stops — FREEZE! Like a statue, like a robot, like a snowman. Nobody move... hold it... hold it...”

    How: Play DJ yourself: stop the music at silly moments, mid-jump if you can. The frozen poses themselves become the show — take a picture of the best statue and let the statue see it after.

  11. 10
    Card 9 · Hide and Seek

    “Hide and seek! One... two... three... (loud, so the hiders can hear) ...nine, TEN! Ready or not, here I come! I wonder where everybody is hiding...”

    How: For threes, hide together at first — you and your child in one spot, giggling, while a grown-up seeks. Teach the house rules kindly: no hiding where doors close, and the curtain behind the sofa always counts.

  12. 11
    Card 10 · Hot Potato

    “Hot potato! Pass it quick, pass it quick — the potato is HOT! Do not hold it, throw it — no wait, pass it gently — quick quick! ...Music stopped! Who has the potato?”

    How: Pass left to start, then try passing right. Speed the music up and the potato gets hotter. The holder of the stopped potato does one funny task — hop three times — and the game rolls on.

  13. Cards 11–20
  14. 12
    Card 11 · Musical Chairs

    “Musical chairs! Walk around the circle — walking feet only, no running — when the music stops, find a chair and SIT! One chair goes away each round... here comes the music...”

    How: For threes, play the kind version: two chairs for the last two players and a shared win, or the left-standing player becomes the DJ who stops the music next round. The job is better than the chair.

  15. 13
    Card 12 · Red Light, Green Light

    “Red light, green light! When I say GREEN LIGHT — run! When I say RED LIGHT — stop like a statue! Green light... RED LIGHT! Nobody move! ...Green light!”

    How: Let your child take the caller job — calling the lights is the best seat in the game. Trick rounds make it comedy: call "red light" in your green voice, and catch every wiggler.

  16. 14
    Card 13 · Bingo

    “Bingo! Look at your card. I call the picture — you find it and cover it! A star... a duck... who has a duck? ...Every square in one row covered? Shout BINGO!”

    How: For first games use picture bingo (the card art does the reading) and call slowly, naming each picture twice. Let your child be the caller for one round — being the voice at the table is its own kind of winning.

  17. 15
    Card 14 · Fishing

    “Fishing time! Hold the rod steady... let the line dangle... wait for it... GOT ONE! You caught the pink fish! Put it in your bucket and pass the rod to the next fisher.”

    How: Make the fish from paper, clip a paper clip on each nose, and tie a magnet to a stick on a string. Count the catch at the end — who caught the most, and who caught the biggest (that one weighs nothing and wins anyway).

  18. 16
    Card 15 · Four in a Row

    “Four in a row! Drop your disc in — clunk! — and I drop mine. Look out: if I get four in a line, I win! Watch the rows AND the slopes — four can hide on an angle.”

    How: First games, play open-book style: point out threats out loud ("uh oh, you have three in a row!") so blocking becomes the game. Once blocking clicks, stop helping and let the strategies go secret.

  19. 17
    Card 16 · Memory Match

    “Memory match! Turn one card... now a second. An apple and an apple — a pair! You keep them! Two different ones? Turn them back and remember where they were...”

    How: Start with just six cards (three pairs) face down — small grids make young memories feel mighty. Grow the grid as the finding gets faster. The proud moment to listen for: "I KNEW where that one was!"

  20. 18
    Card 17 · Rock, Paper, Scissors

    “Rock, paper, scissors — shoot! Make your hand at the same time: a fist is rock, a flat hand is paper, two fingers are scissors. Rock breaks scissors... scissors cut paper... paper covers rock!”

    How: Chant together — "rock, paper, scissors, SHOOT" — the shoot is when hands appear. Best of three makes a fair referee. Then use it the way the playground does: to decide who goes first at everything, all day long.

  21. 19
    Card 18 · Tic-Tac-Toe

    “Tic-tac-toe! You are X and I am O. Put your X in a square — now I put my O somewhere. Three of yours in a row? You win! Three of mine? I win! Watch the diagonals — they are sneaky.”

    How: Draw the grid on paper, or chalk it on the sidewalk and play with rocks and leaves. Teach the block openly at first ("if I get two here, you must go THERE") — then play five quiet rounds and let the strategies become theirs.

  22. 20
    Card 19 · Maze

    “Maze time! Put your finger on START... go slowly... this way... oops, a dead end! Back up and try the other path... there is the FINISH star! You did it!”

    How: Trace with a finger first, then with a pencil once the route is known. Make your own maze for someone else — a few wrong paths drawn on purpose is half the art. Trade mazes and solve each other’s.

  23. 21
    Card 20 · Puzzle

    “Puzzle time! Look at the picture on the box. Find a piece with a flat edge — that is the border! Does this piece fit here? Turn it... try it... click! It belongs!”

    How: Sort pieces into piles before starting: edge pieces, colors, "the ones with the tree". Help for thirty seconds, then hands off — the pride of a finished puzzle only works if the hands doing it are small.

  24. Cards 21–26
  25. 22
    Card 21 · Spot the Difference

    “Spot the difference! Look at the two houses. Same same same... but WAIT — what is different? Look at the sky... look at the trees... count them! How many changes are hiding?”

    How: Play detective: point at each change and say it out loud — "this picture has an extra cloud!" Take turns finding one each. Make your own pair later: draw a simple scene, then copy it with one sneaky change.

  26. 23
    Card 22 · Treasure Hunt

    “Treasure hunt! Here is the first clue: go to the place where we keep the cold milk... the fridge! Look inside — another clue! Follow the trail, clue by clue, until you find the treasure!”

    How: Five clues is a full adventure. Draw simple pictures as clues for pre-readers (a picture of the bookshelf). The treasure matters less than the trail — a single cookie at the end of five clues tastes like gold.

  27. 24
    Card 23 · Charades

    “Charades! I will act like something and you guess what I am. No words from me — only moving! (hop hop hop) What am I? A bunny! Your turn — act like something big...”

    How: Start with animals — they have the clearest movements. Then try actions: brushing teeth, sleeping, kicking a ball. The actor points at guesses to say "warmer" (thumbs up) or "colder" (thumbs down).

  28. 25
    Card 24 · Simon Says

    “Simon says — touch your nose! Simon says — hop on one foot! Now... touch your toes! (no ‘Simon says‘ — did anybody move?) The magic words are SIMON SAYS. Without them, nobody moves!”

    How: Play the leader yourself first, mixing honest commands with three sneaky traps. Then hand over the crown — a child caller learns quickly that the fun is in the trick, not the trap. Fast rounds, big laughs, nobody really out.

  29. 26
    Card 25 · Hopscotch

    “Hopscotch! Throw the stone onto a number — it landed on 4! Now hop the squares: one foot, one foot, two feet, two feet... jump OVER square 4, turn at the top, and hop back to pick it up!”

    How: Draw the course with chalk — numbering the squares 1 to 10 is the first job and the first math. Too hard to hop one-footed? Hop two-footed through the whole course; the course bends to the hopper.

  30. 27
    Card 26 · Jump Rope

    “Jump rope! Swing it over — whoosh — and jump as it comes down! One jump! Again — two jumps! Two friends can turn the rope and chant while you jump: ‘jack be nimble, jack be quick...‘”

    How: First steps without the rope: jump in place to a count. Then hold one handle yourself while a grown-up swings the other side. The double-jump rhythm (rope and feet together) arrives on its own after a dozen tries — celebrate every one.

  31. 28
    Practice

    “Now you are the teacher! Pick any card and tell me what it is.”

    How: Let your child choose the card and say the word in their own way. Teaching someone else is the strongest way to remember.

  32. 29
    Check

    “Can you find Balloon Keep-Up? Now show me Fishing.”

    How: A point, a fetch or the word all count as a pass. If they are unsure, name it for them and try again another day — there are no scores and no pressure.

  33. 30
    Well done

    “Well done! Today we met 26 cards. Let us look for one of them at home.”

    How: End on a win, then spot one of the words in real life today. Meeting it again in the real world is what makes it stay.

Read the script while you show the cards — the say-lines are yours to say out loud and the how-lines are the activity behind each step. Skip, shorten or repeat anything: the class bends to your child, never the other way round.
